messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] RE: inla.mesh.2d failing with boundary argument
parts:
The boundary might be self-intersecting, or “badly” shaped.
Can you provide a picture of it?
If it has too fine detail, the mesher will struggle. A common fix is to set the “cutoff” parameter to remove fine detail.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] RE: inla.mesh.2d failing with boundary argument
parts:
Hi,

this seems to be a much easier problem than it seemed!

The shapefile stores coordinates in a specific CRS which isn't
longitude/latitude. Moreover, it's measured in units=m.

Since you're providing both the shape and long/lat points, and
specifying what ends up being a max.edge of just 40 metres, the mesher
is likely just pending a lot of time adding many many triangles.

If I run it with just the boundary, and max.edge=40e3 (i.e. 40 km), it
finishes quickly.
I don't have the long/lat points you used, but if you really want to
combine these with this boundary, then using the CRS feature for the
mesh itself is a useful option.
In order to avoid problematic numerics due to badly scaled
coordinates, you should also convert the shape to units=km.
The code below works for me:

library(INLA)
library(fields)
library(rgdal)

NE <- readOGR(dsn="NE_ShapeFile", layer="NEstates")

NEcrs.m <- CRS(proj4string(NE))
NEcrs.km <- inla.CRS(NEcrs, args = list(units="km"))
NE.km <- spTransform(NE, CRSobj = NEcrs.km)

## Original version (but without loc), limiting the maximum mesh size:
mesh.NEcrs.m.big <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=NE, max.edge=40,
max.n.strict = 100000L)
mesh.NEcrs.m.big$n
## [1] 100000

## With unit-appropriate max.edge values and specified crs.
## The inla.crs.bounds warning messages can be safely ignored here.
mesh.NEcrs.m <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=NE, max.edge=40e3, crs=NEcrs.m)
mesh.NEcrs.km <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=NE, max.edge=40, crs=NEcrs.km)
mesh.longlat <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=NE, max.edge=0.5, crs=inla.CRS("longlat"))

c(mesh.NEcrs.m$n, mesh.NEcrs.km$n, mesh.longlat$n)
## [1] 695 692 636

plot(mesh.NEcrs.km, asp=1)
plot(mesh.longlat, asp=1)
## Note the difference in shape and orientation.
## It may be better to build the model in the likely
## more isotropic projection instead of longitude-latitude,
## or even in some other projection.
##
## If the mesh has a CRS and the input "loc" is a SpatialPoints object
with a CRS,
## then inla.spde.make.A() will handle the needed projections properly.

## To use "raw data" in longitude/latitude as input to the mesh building,
## you can follow the recipe below.

loc <- data.frame(long = 1:2,lat = 3:4)
coordinates(loc) <- ~ long + lat ## Creates a SpatialPoints object
proj4string(loc) <- inla.CRS("longlat")
loc
## SpatialPoints:
## long lat
## [1,] 1 3
## [2,] 2 4
## Coordinate Reference System (CRS) arguments: +proj=longlat
+ellps=sphere +a=1 +b=1

## To include all the different inputs that live on different projections,
## using any CRS for the mesh itself:
mesh.somecrs <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = loc, boundary=NE, max.edge=1, crs=somecrs)




Finn
